results.pageTitle: Business Intelligence Strategy: A 7-Step Guide for Success (2026)
results.pageDescription: Build a winning business intelligence strategy. This guide covers the key components, steps, and best practices to transform your data into data-driven decisions, improve ROI, and gain a competitive edge in 2026.
results.evidenceText: Business Intelligence Strategy: A 7-Step Guide for Success (2026) Skip to content A business intelligence strategy defines the structure through which data becomes usable: how it’s collected, modeled, governed, and translated into insight that informs action. In large organizations, fragmented pipelines, inconsistent taxonomies, and manual reporting often slow decision cycles and obscure the true performance picture. A well-designed BI strategy eliminates these inefficiencies, ensuring accuracy, scalability, and trust in every metric delivered to the business. This article breaks down how to architect an enterprise-grade BI framework, from data modeling and transformation logic to warehouse integration, metric governance, and visualization alignment. Key Takeaways: Strategy is a Roadmap: A business intelligence strategy is not a single project but a continuous plan that aligns data initiatives with overarching business objectives. Alignment is Everything: The most successful BI strategies are co-created with key business stakeholders to solve specific, high-impact problems. Technology is an Enabler, Not the Goal: The right tools are crucial, but they are only effective when supporting a well-defined strategy and a data-literate culture. Culture Trumps All: Fostering a data-driven culture through training, accessibility, and celebrating wins is essential for long-term user adoption and success. Start with Governance: Establishing clear data governance, quality, and security protocols from the outset prevents future chaos and builds trust in your data. What Is a Business Intelligence (BI) Strategy? A business intelligence strategy is a formal plan that outlines the specific processes, technologies, and cultural frameworks an organization will use to leverage data for improved decision-making. It's the "who, what, when, where, and why" of your entire data analytics ecosystem. This strategic business intelligence approach ensures that every dashboard built, every report generated, and every data point analyzed serves a distinct purpose tied directly to a business outcome. BI Strategy vs. BI Tactic It's crucial to distinguish between strategy and tactics: A BI tactic might be creating a specific sales dashboard or analyzing a single marketing campaign. These are valuable but isolated actions. A BI strategy , in contrast, is the overarching framework that governs these tactics. It defines the rules for data quality, dictates which tools are used, and ensures that the insights from that sales dashboard are shared with the marketing team to inform future campaigns. A strategy provides direction, consistency, and scalability. The Core Components of a Modern BI Strategy A comprehensive BI strategy is built on several key components that work in harmony: Business Objectives: The "why." What specific goals (e.g., increase customer retention by 10%, reduce operational costs by 5%) will BI help achieve? Key Performance Indicators (KPIs): The metrics used to measure progress against objectives. People & Culture: The roles, responsibilities, and training required to create a data-literate organization. This includes executive sponsors, data analysts, and end-users. Data Governance: The policies and procedures for ensuring data is accurate, secure, consistent, and accessible to the right people. Technology & Infrastructure: The tools and platforms for data integration, storage (data warehouses), analysis, and visualization. Implementation Roadmap: A phased plan detailing the timeline, milestones, and resources needed to execute the strategy. The Transformative Impact of an Effective BI Strategy Investing in a well-defined BI strategy is a fundamental business transformation that yields significant returns across the organization. It elevates decision-making from reactive guesswork to proactive, data-informed action. Gaining a Sustainable Competitive Advantage By harnessing BI, companies can identify market trends, anticipate customer needs, and monitor competitor actions with greater speed and accuracy. This intelligence enables you to innovate faster, enter new markets more strategically, and create offerings that truly resonate with your target audience, keeping you several steps ahead of the competition. Enhancing Operational Efficiency and Reducing Costs BI tools illuminate inefficiencies hidden within complex processes. Whether it's optimizing supply chains, streamlining marketing spend, or identifying bottlenecks in the sales funnel, a BI strategy provides the visibility needed to make targeted improvements. This leads directly to reduced waste, lower operational costs, and higher profitability. Fostering Innovation Through Data-Driven Insights Data is the fuel for innovation. A successful BI strategy uncovers previously unseen patterns and correlations, sparking new ideas for products, services, and business models. When employees at all levels have access to reliable data, they are empowered to experiment, test hypotheses, and contribute to the company's growth in meaningful ways. Laying the Groundwork: Pre-Strategy Assessment and Stakeholder Alignment Before you can build a roadmap, you need to know your starting point. A common reason BI initiatives fail is a lack of alignment with the business. This preparatory phase is critical for ensuring your strategy is relevant, supported, and built on a realistic understanding of your organization's capabilities. Identifying Key Business Stakeholders and Champions A BI strategy can’t be developed in an IT silo. It requires active participation from key stakeholders across all major departments, including sales, marketing, finance, and operations. Identify not only the decision-makers but also potential "champions" who are enthusiastic about data and can help drive adoption within their teams. Engaging these stakeholders early and often ensures the strategy addresses real business needs and secures crucial buy-in. Conducting a BI Maturity Assessment Honestly evaluate your organization's current capabilities. Where are you on the BI maturity spectrum? Are you still reliant on manual spreadsheets (nascent), or do you have some departmental dashboards (developing), or are you leveraging predictive analytics (mature)? Understanding your current state helps you set realistic goals and create a phased roadmap that builds capabilities over time. The 7-Step Blueprint for Building Your BI Strategy Roadmap With the groundwork laid, you can now construct the core of your BI strategy. This step-by-step blueprint provides a structured approach to move from concept to a detailed, actionable plan. This is the heart of your business intelligence implementation strategy. Step 1: Define Clear, Measurable Business Objectives and KPIs: Start with the end in mind. Work with your stakeholders to translate high-level business goals into specific, measurable objectives. For example, a goal of "improving marketing effectiveness" becomes an objective like "Increase Marketing Qualified Lead (MQL) to Sales Qualified Lead (SQL) conversion rate by 15% within six months." Then, define the KPIs that will track this, such as conversion rate, cost per SQL, and sales cycle length. Step 2: Assemble a Cross-Functional BI Governance Team: Establish a formal body responsible for overseeing the BI strategy. This team, often called a BI Competency Center (BICC) or data governance council, should include representatives from both business and IT. Their responsibilities include defining data standards, prioritizing BI projects, managing tool selection, and ensuring compliance with security and privacy regulations. Step 3: Select the Right BI and Analytics Technologies: Based on your objectives and user needs, evaluate and select the appropriate technology stack. This includes tools for data extraction and loading (ETL/ELT), data storage, and data analysis and visualization (like Tableau, Power BI, or Looker). Consider factors like ease of use for business users (self-service capabilities), scalability, integration capabilities, and total cost of ownership. Step 4: Develop a Comprehensive Data Management Plan: This plan addresses the entire data lifecycle. It outlines which data sources will be used, how data will be integrated, and the processes for ensuring data quality (cleansing, validation, enrichment). It should also define master data management (MDM) principles to create a "single source of truth" for key entities like customers and products. Step 5: Design a Scalable BI Architecture: This is the technical blueprint for your BI system. It details how data will flow from source systems into a central repository, such as a data warehouse, and then be made available to analytics tools . A well-designed architecture is scalable to handle growing data volumes, flexible to incorporate new data sources, and performant to deliver insights quickly. Step 6: Create an Implementation and Adoption Roadmap: Break the strategy down into manageable phases. A typical approach is to start with a pilot project that addresses a high-impact, low-complexity business problem to demonstrate early value. The roadmap should outline a timeline for subsequent phases, including specific deliverables, resource allocation, and a detailed training and change management plan to drive user adoption. Step 7: Establish a Framework for Measuring ROI: To secure ongoing investment and support, you must prove the value of your BI strategy. Develop a framework to measure its return on investment (ROI). This can include hard metrics like cost savings and revenue increases, as well as soft metrics like time saved on manual reporting, faster decision-making, and improved employee satisfaction. Struggling With Step 5? Let Improvado Handle the Architecture Designing a scalable BI system is complex—but it doesn’t have to be. Improvado unifies data from every marketing, sales, and revenue source, automates modeling and transformation, and delivers clean, governed datasets ready for analysis. Build a flexible, future-proof BI architecture without the engineering burden. Get your demo Choosing Your Technology: BI Tools and Platforms Comparison The BI tool market is vast and varied. Selecting the right platform is a critical decision that directly impacts user adoption and the overall success of your strategy. The primary choice often lies between traditional, IT-led platforms and modern, self-service tools that empower business users. Key Features to Look for in a BI Tool Data Connectivity: The ability to easily connect to a wide range of sources, from databases and cloud applications to spreadsheets. Data Visualization: A rich library of charts, graphs, and maps with interactive drill-down capabilities. Ease of Use: An intuitive, drag-and-drop interface that allows non-technical users to build their own reports and dashboards. Collaboration & Sharing: Features that allow users to share insights, comment on dashboards, and schedule report delivery. Governance & Security: Robust administrative controls for managing user access, data security, and content certification. Scalability: The ability to handle large datasets and a growing number of users without performance degradation. The implementation phase is where the strategic vision meets operational reality. Focusing on these critical pillars ensures a smoother rollout and greater long-term success. Data Governance and Security Protocols Data governance is the foundation of trust in your BI system. Without it, you risk a "garbage in, garbage out" scenario where users don't trust the data and abandon the tools. Establish clear ownership for key data assets, define standard business metrics, and implement robust security protocols to control data access based on user roles and responsibilities. Data Integration and Quality Management Your BI platform is only as powerful as the data it contains. The biggest challenge for many organizations is integrating data from dozens of disparate sources. This is where modern data pipeline platforms become essential, automating the process of combining information from various systems. This process must also include rigorous data quality checks to cleanse, de-duplicate, and standardize data for accurate analysis. Improvado addresses this challenge by providing an end-to-end data infrastructure purpose-built for analytics and BI teams. It automates extraction, transformation, and loading (ETL/ELT) of marketing, sales, and revenue data into your preferred warehouse. Beyond aggregation, Improvado enforces governance rules, maintains schema consistency, and performs quality validation at every stage of the pipeline. With Improvado, you can: Connect to 1,400+ data sources with fully automated data extraction. Normalize and standardize metrics and dimensions across channels for consistent BI reporting. Enforce naming conventions and data governance policies to maintain structural integrity. Apply automated validation, anomaly detection, and error handling for continuous data accuracy. Deliver clean, BI-ready datasets directly into warehouses like BigQuery, Snowflake, or Redshift. Maintain full data lineage and transparency across every transformation step. Access unified datasets instantly through the AI Agent, using natural language queries for ad-hoc insight generation, or use pre-build dashboard templates for Tableau, Looker Studio and Power BI. Build a Reliable Data Foundation for BI at Scale Improvado automates data integration, transformation, and quality assurance across all your marketing, sales, and revenue systems. With governed pipelines and real-time validation, it delivers trusted, warehouse-ready data your BI team can rely on for accurate, enterprise-grade reporting. Get your demo Building Effective and Actionable KPI Dashboards Dashboards are the primary interface between users and data. A poorly designed dashboard can be just as confusing as a raw spreadsheet. The best practice is to design dashboards that tell a story, starting with high-level summaries and allowing users to drill down into details. Effective KPI dashboards are tailored to specific roles and focus on the metrics that matter most for their decision-making process. Waleed Noury Lead Analytics Engineer at Activision Overcoming Common Challenges in BI Strategy Execution Even the best-laid plans encounter obstacles. Being aware of the common challenges in BI implementation allows you to address them proactively rather than being derailed by them. Tackling Data Silos and Poor Data Quality: This is arguably the most common and difficult challenge. It requires both a technical solution (data integration platforms) and an organizational one (fostering cross-departmental collaboration). Managing Change and Ensuring User Adoption: People are naturally resistant to change. A comprehensive change management plan, including communication, training, and support, is not optional – it's essential for success. Balancing Agility with Governance: Business users want speed and flexibility, while IT needs to ensure security and data integrity. A successful strategy finds the right balance, often by creating a "governed self-service" model. Proving Value and Sustaining Executive Sponsorship: Initial enthusiasm can wane if the BI initiative doesn't show tangible results. Continuously track and communicate wins, tying them back to the original business objectives and ROI framework. Best Practices for Long-Term BI Success and Evolution A BI strategy is not a "set it and forget it" document. The business landscape and technology are constantly changing, and your strategy must evolve with them. Adopting these best practices ensures your BI program remains relevant and valuable for the long term. Adopt an Agile and Iterative Approach Avoid massive, multi-year "big bang" projects. Instead, adopt an agile methodology, delivering value in small, iterative cycles. This allows you to gather user feedback early, adapt to changing requirements, and demonstrate progress continuously. Continuously Align BI with Evolving Business Goals Schedule regular reviews (e.g., quarterly) of your BI strategy with key stakeholders. Are the original objectives still relevant? Have new business priorities emerged? This ensures your BI efforts remain focused on what matters most to the organization. Automate Where Possible for Efficiency Manual data preparation and reporting are time-consuming and prone to error. Leverage reporting automation to free up your analysts from mundane tasks so they can focus on higher-value activities like deep-dive analysis and interpreting insights. This significantly increases the efficiency and scalability of your analytics team. Integrate Advanced Analytics and Marketing Attribution As your BI program matures, move beyond descriptive analytics (what happened) to more advanced forms. This includes incorporating diagnostic analytics (why it happened) and predictive analytics (what will happen). For marketers, this means implementing sophisticated models like multi-touch marketing attribution to understand the true impact of every channel. The Future of Business Intelligence: Trends Shaping Enterprise BI Strategy The field of BI is rapidly evolving, driven by advancements in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and cloud computing. A forward-thinking enterprise BI strategy must account for these trends to maintain a competitive edge. The Rise of AI and Machine Learning in BI AI is transforming BI from a reactive tool to a proactive partner. Augmented analytics uses machine learning to automatically surface hidden insights, identify anomalies, and even suggest actions. This makes sophisticated data analysis accessible to a broader audience, reducing the need for specialized data science skills for many common tasks. Predictive and Prescriptive Analytics The future of BI lies in not just understanding the past, but in predicting the future and prescribing the best course of action. Predictive models can forecast sales, identify customers at risk of churn, and optimize inventory levels. Prescriptive analytics takes this a step further by recommending specific actions to achieve desired outcomes. The Growing Importance of Real-Time Analytics In a fast-paced digital world, decisions must be made in minutes, not days. The ability to analyze streaming data from sources like IoT devices, web traffic, and social media analytics in real-time is becoming a critical capability for industries like e-commerce, logistics, and finance. Integrating all of these sources, including your data warehouse, is key to a holistic view. Conclusion A strong business intelligence strategy begins and ends with data. results.title: Layercake.graphics framework for Svelte
results.pageDescription: A framework for mostly-reusable graphics with svelte
results.evidenceText: Layer Cake Menu Layer Cake All Client-side Bar Beeswarm Beeswarm, force layout Brush Calendar Circle pack Circle pack, force layout Cleveland dot plot Column annotated Diverging bar Diverging column Grouped bar Grouped column Histogram Line + area Map Multilayer map Multiline Nested circle pack Radar chart Sankey Scatter Small multiples Stacked area Stacked bar Stacked column Synced brush Time of day plot WebGL Scatter Server-side Bar Brush Calendar Cleveland dot plot Column annotated Diverging bar Diverging column Grouped bar Grouped column Histogram Line + area Map Multilayer map Multiline Scatter Small multiples Stacked area Stacked bar Stacked column Synced brush Time of day plot WebGL Scatter Layer Cake Layer Cake is a headless graphics framework for Svelte . It uses the measurements of your target div and your data extents to create scales that stay synced on layout changes. Use these scales to organize multiple, mostly-reusable Svelte components , whether they be SVG, HTML, Canvas or WebGL. Since they all share the same coordinate space, you can build your graphic one layer at a time. It can also be used to easily create responsive graphics server-side that work without JavaScript . Unlike other libraries, chart components live inside your project , so you have complete control for customization . It also includes some handy helper functions to help format your data into the right shape. Read the guide , try the starter template or check out the example components . See the examples below and even edit them live. Here's a sample of what the code looks like: Looking for the version 10 examples that used the store API? They're at the v10 documentation archive . < script > // The library provides a main wrapper component // and a bunch of empty layout components... import { LayerCake , Svg , Html , Canvas } from 'layercake' ; // ...that you fill with your own chart components, // that live inside your project and which you // can copy and paste from here as starting points. import AxisX from './components/AxisX.svelte' ; import AxisY from './components/AxisY.svelte' ; import Line from './components/Line.svelte' ; import Scatter from './components/Scatter.svelte' ; import Labels from './components/Labels.svelte' ; const data = [{ x : 0 , y : 1 }, { x : 1 , y : 2 }, { x : 2 , y : 3 }]; </ script > < style > .chart-container { width : 100% ; height : 500px ; } </ style > < div class = "chart-container" > < LayerCake x = 'x' y = 'y' {data} > < Svg > < AxisX /> < AxisY /> < Line color = '#f0c' /> </ Svg > < Canvas > < Scatter color = '#0fc' /> </ Canvas > < Html > < Labels /> </ Html > </ LayerCake > </ div > Line + area WebGL Scatter (svg axes, quadtree hover) Map (svg, tooltip, pre-projected) Multilayer map (canvas + svg) Column annotated Stacked column Grouped column Grouped bar Bar Stacked bar Diverging column Diverging bar Multiline (html labels + quadtree tooltip) Stacked area Scatter (svg + canvas + voronoi) Cleveland dot plot Calendar (one cake per month) Time of day plot Histogram (variable bins) 40 bins Small multiples (animated domain transition) Individual scale Shared scale Radar chart Circle pack Nested circle pack Sankey Brush Synced brush Beeswarm Beeswarm, force layout Circle pack, force layout Group by category Clump together Server-side rendering Svelte makes it easy to render your project server side and Layer Cake has built-in helpers to make it even easier for charts. All of these examples below (except for their canvas components) will load and be responsive without client-side JavaScript. The advantage is that you can see the chart as soon as the page loads, avoiding blank placeholder spaces. HTML charts use percentage-based scales and SVG charts take advantage of certain viewBox and CSS settings that Rich Harris, Svelte's creator, outlined in this blog post . For shapes that are difficult to render using percentages, such as swoopy arrows, Layer Cake makes it easy to superimpose client-side components that will hydrate once JavaScript is available. See the annotated column example below. results.pageTitle: Which fonts to use for your charts and tables | Datawrapper Blog
results.pageDescription: Sans-serif or serif typefaces? Lining or oldstyle figures? Narrow or wide? With lots of examples, we explain which fonts work best for data visualizations.
results.evidenceText: Which fonts to use for your charts and tables | Datawrapper Blog Skip to main content This article is brought to you by Datawrapper , a data visualization tool for creating charts , maps , and tables . Learn more . All Blog Categories How should the text appear in your data visualizations? The possibilities are endless: There are millions of typefaces out there (Arial, Times New Roman, Lato, ...) belonging to different categories (serif, sans-serif, condensed, wide, ...). Many of these typefaces come in different fonts (thin, bold, ...). And then they are so many extra ways of adjusting them (uppercase, size, color, ...). The short answer: When in doubt, set your text in a font that's easy to read. Easy to read is everything that readers are used to. On the web, that means sans-serif , neither overly narrow nor wide , regular (instead of bold or thin) text set in sentence case , in a size that's big enough to read, and in black or almost black. This article explains all these options — and shows how ignoring this advice can set your visualization apart from others. Choosing a font 01 Use sans-serif typefaces. 02 Use a font with lining and tabular numbers. 03 Use a font with all the symbols you need. 04 Use bold fonts only for emphasis. 05 Avoid very thin fonts. 06 Use neither overly narrow nor overly wide fonts. Adjusting the font 07 Use text that's big enough. 08 Use a high-contrast color for most text. 09 Use uppercase text sparingly . Let's start: Choosing a font Use sans-serif typefaces. Serif typefaces (like Times New Roman or Georgia ) bring you into a reading flow — that’s why they’re great for setting long texts like novels or newspaper articles. For data visualizations, sans-serif (”without serifs”) typefaces are most often the better choice. They look cleaner and are often easier to skim than serif fonts, especially when it comes to numbers. Our free Datawrapper visualizations , for example, use the sans-serif typeface Roboto . Changing the fonts – including size, placement, color, etc. – in Datawrapper is possible with a custom theme . Most data visualizations use sans-serif typefaces — like all charts from The Economist and Bloomberg: The Economist, 2022. Fonts: Econ Sans and Econ Sans Condensed. Join the community Back to resources - help tab section Back to tabs Frequently asked questions Expand all Collapse all 01/ What is Power BI and what’s it used for? Power BI is a unified, scalable platform for self-service and enterprise business intelligence (BI). You can use it to connect to and visualize any data, and infuse the visuals into the apps you use every day. 02/ What is a business intelligence platform? A business intelligence platform is a tool that connects, analyzes, and visualizes data so organizations can make better decisions. With Power BI, this means turning your data into interactive dashboards and insights that help teams understand performance and take action faster. 03/ How should I choose a Power BI license for my organization? Power BI licenses aren’t exclusive—there are several ways to mix and match plans and licenses. For example, you could purchase Premium (P-SKU) or Microsoft Fabric (F-SKU) capacity to host the most popular reports, and then buy Power BI Pro licenses (or get them through Microsoft 365 E5) for your users who need to create and publish reports. Contact a sales expert to learn more. Contact sales 04/ What is Power BI Embedded? Microsoft Power BI Embedded is a pay-as-you-go platform as a service (PaaS) offering. It allows app developers to embed fully interactive reports into their apps without having to build their own data visuals and controls. Power BI Embedded costs as little as $1 per hour for analytics, with no requirement for end-user licensing. Try Power BI Embedded 05/ What’s the difference between Microsoft Fabric and Power BI? Microsoft Fabric is an end-to-end analytics solution with full-service capabilities including data movement, data lakes, data engineering, data integration, data science, real-time analytics, data monitoring, and business intelligence—all backed by a shared platform providing robust data security, governance, and compliance. Power BI provides the business intelligence layer in Microsoft Fabric that enables you to gain insights from your data. Power BI Premium customers can simply turn on the Fabric tenant setting and access the rest of the product in a unified experience. And with its unified capacity model, Power BI Premium per capacity can be used against any Microsoft Fabric workload. 06/ Can I access Microsoft Fabric if I'm a Power BI Pro customer? Power BI Pro customers can access Fabric workloads only through the Microsoft Fabric trial experience. Try Microsoft Fabric 07/ What features are available in Fabric SKUs compared to Power BI SKUs? Feature availability depends on both SKU and capacity level. See the features list for specific details. 08/ Are there free Power BI training and certifications available for my team? Yes, Microsoft offers free, self-paced Power BI training through Microsoft Learn, with structured learning paths that cover everything from getting started to building reports and modeling data. You can also take practice assessments to prepare for official certifications once your team is ready. Explore learning paths 09/ What are some Power BI dashboard examples? Microsoft provides a wide range of Power BI dashboard examples to help you get started. On Microsoft Learn, you can explore and download sample reports across scenarios like sales, customer profitability, IT spend, HR, and more, giving you a clear view of how dashboards are built and used. results.evidenceText: Selenium For AI agents: the site's llms.txt is at /llms.txt. Automate any browser, from any language. Selenium is a browser automation tool that gives you full control over Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari. Write your scripts in Java, Python, C#, Ruby, JavaScript or Kotlin using the official W3C WebDriver standard . Get started Using AI agents Works out of the box: Selenium downloads what it needs to talk to your browser, so there is nothing to install by hand. Install Selenium and run your first script Add the Selenium package for your language, then run the script below. It opens Chrome, loads a page and closes the browser again. Java Python CSharp Ruby JavaScript Kotlin Add org.seleniumhq.selenium:selenium-java to your build, then run: package dev.selenium.hello ; import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver ; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver ; public class HelloSelenium { public static void main ( String [] args ) { WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver (); driver . get ( "https://selenium.dev" ); driver . quit (); } } View on GitHub Install the package: pip install selenium Then run: from selenium import webdriver driver = webdriver . Chrome () driver . get ( "http://selenium.dev" ) driver . quit () View on GitHub Install the package: dotnet add package Selenium.WebDriver Then run: using OpenQA.Selenium.Chrome ; namespace SeleniumDocs.Hello ; public static class HelloSelenium { public static void Main () { var driver = new ChromeDriver (); driver . Navigate (). GoToUrl ( "https://selenium.dev" ); driver . Quit (); } } View on GitHub Install the gem: gem install selenium-webdriver Then run: # frozen_string_literal: true require 'selenium-webdriver' driver = Selenium :: WebDriver . for :chrome driver . get 'https://selenium.dev' driver . quit View on GitHub Install the package: npm install selenium-webdriver Then run: const { Builder , Browser } = require ( 'selenium-webdriver' ); ( async function helloSelenium () { let driver = await new Builder (). forBrowser ( Browser . CHROME ). build (); await driver . get ( 'https://selenium.dev' ); await driver . quit (); })(); View on GitHub Kotlin uses the Java bindings. Add org.seleniumhq.selenium:selenium-java to your build, then run: package dev.selenium.hello import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver fun main () { val driver = ChromeDriver () driver . get ( "https://selenium.dev" ) driver . quit () } View on GitHub Need more detail? Follow the Getting Started guide . Pick your tool Selenium WebDriver Use this when you want to drive a browser from code in your own language. WebDriver is a collection of language-specific bindings that control a real browser the way a user would, and it is the foundation for everything else Selenium does. Read more Selenium Grid Use this when you need to run your WebDriver tests on several machines, browsers and operating systems at once. Grid distributes sessions from a central point so you can run against a vast combination of environments in parallel. results.title: Part 2: Let the Data Breathe
results.pageDescription: Making Internet Things, Part 2: Design.
results.evidenceText: Making Internet Things, Part 2: Design Skip to main content How to Make Dope Shit Part 2: Design This is the second installment of a multi-part series designed to help you familiarize yourself with the tools used to make visual, data-driven essays. By Ilia Blinderman Introduction A few months ago, I put together the first part of a guide to help people who wanted to start delving into that hard-to-pin-down brand of storytelling that we do at The Pudding. I was frustrated by the fact that finding sufficiently beginner-friendly resources was so difficult, and decided to collect the most useful links for jumping into data analysis in this blog post . Today, I bring you the second installment of How To Make Dope Shit on The Internet; this one, aimed at helping ease some anxieties that people may have about designing visualizations. Design and Data Visualization Approaching the design of a visualization can be daunting: which insights of your analysis will you visualize? Which chart should you use? How will you code it? The complexity of this chain of decisions can quickly become frustrating. Picking the right way to communicate data may be difficult enough on its own, but pairing it with code, especially when you’re new to programming, can seem exponentially more maddening. I get it — I’ve been there, and that uncertainty sucks. Below, I’ll provide you with a few thoughts on how to make this a little less anxiety-inducing, because at the end of the day, you’re doing cool, exciting work. Look at visualization To learn how to create something, you need to see what others who were practicing it before you were doing. Ernest Hemingway read the works of Shakespeare and Dostoyevsky; Picasso deconstructed the paintings of Velázquez and Goya. While we’re not in the same league, or even playing the same game, the core principle remains the same. In order to know what’s possible — both in terms of what to visualize and how to do it — draw inspiration from past pieces of data visualization that you’ve seen and enjoyed. Internally, we’re always getting excited about work that our peers are putting out. Some of our most consistent sources of inspiration are: The New York Times’ interactives The Upshot The Washington Post Google News Lab The Guardian's interactives The r/dataisbeautiful subreddit I’d also suggest you take some time exploring the archives of Kantar’s Information Is Beautiful Awards , which view like an encyclopedia of some of the best-designed visualizations in the past several years. Another terrific resource is Andy Kirk’s Visualizing Data , which contains a massive monthly archive of his favourite visualizations. Archive the work that you like I frequently come across data viz work that I admire, either due to the clarity of its message, the aesthetic design, or certain subtle touches that solve visual problems I’ve previously struggled to overcome. Since you’re likely to be learning viz on the fly, either while you’re working on a technical project or in your spare time, it’s imperative to keep notes on the most interesting and impressive pieces you encounter. To make sure that I remember the lessons to be gleaned from each of these, I save them to an ever-open Google doc. It’s as simple as taking a screenshot and adding it to the doc with an annotation of what I liked about it, and a link to the original. Another option is to use Sightline , a tool created by Jordan Sechler and Evan Peck, which allows you to automatically save data visualizations you encounter online through a Chrome extension. In addition to automatically compiling your personal archive, you can explore the visualizations that have been saved by other users, which makes trawling for inspiration even easier. Think about your message Before you begin visualizing your data, think through the most important points that you’re trying to communicate. Is the key message the growth of a variable over time? A disparity between quantities? The degree to which a particular value varies? A geographic pattern? Once you have an idea of the essential takeaways you’d like your readers to understand, you can consider which type of visualization would be most effective at expressing it. During this step, I like to think of the pieces of work that I’ve got in my archive and see if any one of those is especially suitable for the task at hand. Other freely available resources are the Data Viz Catalogue or Data Viz Project , which give a long list of chart examples, alongside descriptions of the types of data they’re most suited to. Don’t design in code Once you’ve got a chart in mind, it’s time to design it out. Some people can sketch a few lines on the back of a napkin and jump straight to code, designing as they go (I’m looking at you, Russell ). For most people reading this guide, however, designing on the fly in JavaScript isn’t a viable option: it’s too easy to get bogged down in bugs and syntax, going down StackOverflow rabbit holes rather than designing viz. Instead, I’d recommend spending some time designing the static visualizations using a simpler tool. This will allow you to quickly get a sense of whether or not your visualization communicates the insights you’re hoping to express. There’s no need for coding or fancy software, here. For years, Matt’s been drafting viz in Keynote , and quickly converted me to doing so after we began to work together. It’s surprisingly easy to create data-driven charts and fine-tune their design using Keynote’s in-built capabilities (shapes, masks, gradients, etc.), while keeping the learning curve sufficiently low and avoiding barriers posed by more powerful software like Adobe Illustrator (if you’re comfortable with Illustrator, bless your heart — go forth and design the hell out of your viz, but remember not to get too bogged down in detail). We've also recently started to explore Figma , a web-based design tool that makes it easy to collaborate with multiple team members and helps export CSS styles, and have been thoroughly impressed. Happy with the viz you’ve designed, and itching to make it interactive? Let’s talk code. Ready to learn to code, pt. 1: Read Scott Murray’s Book There are very few resources for learning to code data-driven visualizations that are geared for beginners, and Scott Murray’s Interactive Data Visualization for the Web is one of the few that explains a sufficiently broad range of concepts to get you started with programming. I read his original book cover to cover, and can testify to the fact that it was an incredibly useful resource when it came to helping me understand both general HTML/CSS, and the way that D3, the JavaScript library that we use for data-driven visualizations, works. Moreover, Murray does a terrific job of limiting the concepts he exposes his readers to, which helps beginners bypass the “Dear god there’s so much I don’t understand, EJECT!” stage. I can’t recommend it enough. Ready to learn to code, pt. 2: Look at other people’s code Ian Johnson, known online as enjalot, has created a wonderfully useful tool for browsing data-driven visualizations called Bl.ock Builder . Want to put together a pie chart but aren’t sure how? Just search for “pie” and browse any one of the numerous code examples. Confused by how to use the d3.forceSimulation function? Search for “d3.force” and read through the code — most of the time, you should be able to find a code example that will help you get your head around the tricky concepts. Ready to learn to code, pt. 3: Ask questions! Sometimes, learning how to combine all of these skills can be a lonely endeavour, and it may seem like there’s no one around to help. In truth, the data visualization community is incredibly helpful and supportive. If you get stuck, or just want to talk about coding and visualization with other folks in the same boat, the D3 Slack group can be a great resource. For more pointed technical questions without the camaraderie, posting a question tagged with d3.js posts on StackOverflow is a quick way to clear up any technical ambiguities you’re struggling with. Putting it all together My hope is that the previous sections have helped with any specific design and coding questions you may have faced. Nevertheless, combining all of these steps to create a final output is hard if you’re not used to doing so. That’s why I’d like to leave you with a few examples of the fact that even for pros, design is hard, time-consuming, and iterative. Check out, for example, this image that Scientific American’s Jen Christiansen tweeted out , documenting the numerous design drafts that her team produced to demonstrate the stages of pregnancy: AXS Studio (Contributors: Man-San Ma, Sonya Amin, Eddy Xuan, Joyce Hui, and Susan Park); Jen Christiansen (art direction) The evolution from original concept to final form is dramatic, and I love the fact that Jan, who’s been working at Scientific American for over a decade, puts so much emphasis on honing her team’s designs over a series of steps. Our team has done the same. Consider Matt’s lengthy design process for our collaboration with Google News Lab, examining the diversity in US newsrooms (final project available here ). First, there was the initial whiteboard session: After this, he created a multitude of different designs for the various sections of the project: To see how the final version turned out, head here . Finally, I’d like to leave you with a talk by Mike Bostock, who created the D3 library that we rely on so consistently to produce our visualizations, and who spent several years creating visualizations at the New York Times. Here, he discusses the fact that designing visualizations is a matter of work. While good design may be an innate talent for a select few, most of us are in the same boat: quality work is a function of hours invested, rather than preternatural skill. Seeing the many iterations of Mike’s work is, to me, thoroughly heartening: if someone of his calibre tries a hundred different approaches to see what sticks, it’s a good signal to the rest of us to keep our noses to the grindstone.

results.pageDescription: The Creative Code Intensive is a 12-week in-person course at Gray Area in San Francisco, designed for artists, designers, and technologists looking to expand their creative practice with AI, machine learning, and interactive media. Through hands-on coding, experimentation, and critical engagement, participants will develop interactive projects that culminate in a public showcase attended by industry professionals and the creative community. The 2026 curriculum introduces AI and Machine Learning, alongside fundamentals in physical computing, creative coding, audiovisual performance, and interactive web applications. Participants will explore fine-tuning AI models, generative tools, and creative computation, all while building a portfolio of 10+ projects. Scholarships available | Apply by Fe
results.evidenceText: Creative Code Intensive - Gray Area Creative Code Intensive Apply for the Intensive: Where creative studio practice meets Computer Science Our Creative Code Intensive is a 12-week course in creative technology, offering a comprehensive introduction to foundational and advanced tools for programming interactive experiences. Guided by expert instructors, participants gain technical skills and creative inspiration to design, prototype, and install an interactive experience or artwork in a public showcase attended by the creative community, technology industry, and museum professionals. The 2026 curriculum incorporates Physical Computing alongside emerging technologies. Participants will critically explore generative artificial intelligence tools and introducing core concepts for building machine learning models. The course also emphasizes the fundamentals of computer programming for creative media, audiovisual performance, and interactive applications for the web . Through playful experimentation, Gray Area’s Creative Code Intensive encourages participants to both embrace and interfere with new technologies as a mode of critical engagement, fostering creativity through technological experimentation and exploration. Whether you’re an artist exploring new tools, a designer crafting interactive media, or an industry professional advancing your AI expertise, this interdisciplinary course will provide opportunities to expand your skills and prepare you for new career pathways in creative technology.  Application deadline extended! Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis through February 22 APPLY TO THE CREATIVE CODE INTENSIVE Learning Outcomes Students in the course will: Apply coding fundamentals  (e.g., variables, loops, conditionals, functions, arrays, objects) to create visual and interactive media Practice advanced coding topics (e.g. handling user input, networked communications, object modeling, machine learning) through hands-on creative projects Recognize and debug technical issues in code Develop a creative voice by building time-based works, live performances, and interactive applications Engage with emerging technologies including Artificial Intelligence and examine their potential, limitations, and risks Contextualize their work in the fields of creative code, media arts, and technology Present and critique​ their own creative work and provide constructive feedback on the work of others Plan, scope, and execute complex technical projects Apply workforce-ready skills such as project planning, advanced technical proficiency, and professional presentation techniques Prepare and showcase professional-grade projects in a final public exhibition, including installation and documentation Program Features Creative and professional development for technical and design skills Hands-on practice writing and debugging software Over 100 hours of classroom instruction Production of a portfolio of 10+ creative code projects Access to a network of hundreds of peers, alumni, and professionals to build connections with potential collaborators and employers Affordable enrollment fee of $4,500 (monthly payment terms are available) Scholarships available for students, prioritized by need Dates & Program Details 2026 Spring Session: In-Person March 3rd – May 9th, 2026 Showcase Opens: May 20, 2026 Tuesdays & Thursdays (6–9pm) & Saturdays (11am–3pm) Classes are held in-person at: Gray Area / Grand Theater 2665 Mission St San Francisco, CA 94110 Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis until the class is filled. Apply by February 22, 2026 for fullest consideration. Accessibility: Please note that this workshop will be held in the upstairs Gray Area classroom, which is not ADA accessible . We apologize for any inconvenience and encourage those impacted to contact us for assistance. Thank you for your understanding. Reach out to [email protected] with any questions. Syllabus Week 1: Drawing and Interaction with p5.js Week 2: Machine Learning with ml5.js Week 3: Building Websites with HTML & CSS Week 4: JavaScript & the Document Object Model Week 5: Audiovisual Performance with Hydra and Projection Mapping Week 6: Web Audio Week 7: Physical Computing 1: Inputs Week 8: Physical Computing 2: Outputs Week 9: Generative Text with LLMs and node.js Week 10: Prototyping Interactive Environments Week 11: Project Development Week Week 12: Final Project Public Showcase Prerequisites The pace of the course requires that students enter the class with some foundational programming knowledge. We recommend that applicants have some practice working with concepts covered in Code! Programming with p5.js and HTML/CSS/DOM on The Coding Train to be successful in this course. These tutorials are excellent starting points for beginners who need more practice before enrolling in this course. APPLY TO THE CREATIVE CODE INTENSIVE Diversity Scholarship To help creators of all backgrounds reach their goals, we are proud to offer a diversity scholarship to sustain and advance an inclusive community at Gray Area and beyond. This scholarship is for outstanding students from diverse backgrounds that are underrepresented in higher education and the fields of art, design, and technology. Recipients will receive a $450–$1125 discount towards partial tuition for our bi-annual Creative Code Intensive Program. The Diversity Scholarship prioritizes applicants who are women, queer, gender nonconforming folks, and people of color. We highly encourage students to apply for this scholarship. Student Showcase Every Creative Code Intensive session culminates with a media arts exhibition, showcasing work from students alongside artists in our Incubator program. This highly attended event invites the public and industry leaders to see new work from our artist community. See some previous examples from final showcases below. Visit Our Spring 2022 showcase Over 250 alumni have joined the Immersive and our private email list which provides upcoming opportunities. Watch a testimonial below from one of our alumni. Creative Code Intensive Project: “Water Pixels” by Francis Li Instructor(s) Kate Hollenbach Education Director Kate Hollenbach is an artist, programmer, and educator. She is passionate about using open source tools and teaching in interdisciplinary environments where art and technology meet. Before joining Gray Area, Kate was an Assistant Professor of Emergent Digital Practices at the University of Denver. She is also a contributor to p5.js and serves as an advisor to the Processing Foundation. In her creative practice, Kate creates video and interactive works examining critical issues in user interface and user experience design with a focus on user habits, data collection, and surveillance. Her work is informed by years of professional experience as an interface designer and product developer. She has presented, published, and exhibited work in venues such as the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, SIGGRAPH, INST-INT, Piksel Festival, and Taper Zine. Jeffrey Hawkins Jeffrey Hawkins is an education and data visualization expert with a PhD in physics focusing on physics education research. He has worked with organizations ranging from leading design studios to Head Start programs in developing data visualizations for use in education, community building and other domains. Recently he has present artworks utilizing technology and AI at Art Hack Day and Fidget Camp Showcase. Additionally, he also has a decade of experience teaching physics at the university level and leading education research projects. Leia Chang Leia S. Chang (they/them) is an artist, organizer, and creative technologist exploring unusual materiality and embodied identity. With a strong command over creative fabrication, Leia channels their perspective as a second-generation Chinese-American into interactive installations, poetic texts, and tangible multi-media objects made of wood, resin, and found materials. Their work often integrates digital media into physical forms with the aim of spotlighting the connection between memory, identity, and storytelling. Leia is currently an exhibit developer at the Exploratorium in San Francisco. Their work has been shown at the likes of La Mama’s CultureHub, theBlanc Art Space, the Gray Area SF and Resistor NYC. They organize creative communities and facilitate workshops on making-as-art. Celeste Betancur Celeste Betancur is a researcher at Stanford University’s Center for Computer Research in Music and Acoustics (CCRMA), where her research explores the intersections of music, technology, and algorithmic composition. As a composer, digital artist, and live coder, her work spans a broad spectrum—from academic concert halls to underground electronic music scenes—emphasizing real-time score generation, live coding performance, and the development of interactive audiovisual systems. Her interdisciplinary practice includes the design and construction of expanded musical instruments, large-scale installations, and sculptures. Betancur’s compositions have been performed by internationally renowned ensembles such as A Far Cry, Leimay Ensemble, Distractfold Ensemble, Cinevivo, Andamio, Iran Sanadzadeh, Niloufar Shiri, Adapter Ensemble, RGGTRN, Linea Ensemble and many others. Beyond composition and performance, Betancur is an accomplished software developer specializing in music technology. She has contributed and is actively working for the ChucK programming language development. Her performances have taken place across more than 20 countries. She has presented her research at leading international conferences such as NeurIPS, ICLC, ICMC, SMC, and NIME, contributing to the ongoing dialogue at the intersection of music, computation, and artistic expression. results.pageTitle: What to consider when choosing colors for data visualization | Datawrapper Blog
results.pageDescription: A first overview with the most important do
results.evidenceText: What to consider when choosing colors for data visualization | Datawrapper Blog Skip to main content This article is brought to you by Datawrapper , a data visualization tool for creating charts , maps , and tables . Learn more . All Blog Categories Data Visualisation can be defined as representing numbers with shapes – and no matter what these shapes look like (areas, lines, dots), they need to have a color. Sometimes colors just make the shapes visible, sometimes they encode data or categories themselves. We’ll focus mostly on the latter in this article. But we’ll also take a general look at colors and what to consider when choosing them: When to use colors in data visualization Consider if there is a better alternative to gradient colors when encoding your most important values.  Gradient colors can be great to show a pattern, e.g. on a choropleth map, but it’s hard to decipher the actual values from them and to see differences between the values. Consider showing your most important values with bars, position (like in a dot plot) or even areas, and to use colors to only show categories. Readers will be able to decipher your values faster: If you need more than seven colors in a chart, consider using another chart type or to group categories together.  Colors make it easy to let readers distinguish between categories in your data, but try to avoid using more than seven of them. The more colors in a chart represent your data, the harder it becomes to read it quickly. Your readers will need to often consult the color key to understand what is shown in your chart. Consider using another chart type: How to make better color choices Consider using the same color for the same variables.  If you just use one color for all your charts, using the same color is the best option to make your article not overly colorful. For example, it’s ok to show the unemployment rate in blue in the first chart and a few paragraphs later a GDP chart with the same color. However, if you use more than one color for your first chart, the colors in this chart will be “taken”. To not confuse readers and increase comparability, consider only using these colors again if you’re showing data about the same category/country/etc.: Make sure to explain to readers what your colors encode.  Every visual mark that represents a value or variable should be explained: What does the height of your bar mean? What does the size of your circles on a symbol map represent? The same is true for colors. There are many ways to create a color key. Here are three of them: Consider the color grey as the most important color in Data Vis.  Using grey for less important elements in your chart makes your highlight colors (which should be reserved for your most important data points) stick out even more. Grey is also helpful for general context data, less important annotations, to show what’s unselected by the user, or to calm down the overall visual impression of your charts. Since grey can seem a bit cold, consider using it with a hint of color: Try a warm grey (grey+yellow/orange/red), or use another very light color as an alternative (e.g. super light yellow): Make sure your contrasts are high enough.  Caring about contrast means caring if your readers will be able to read your chart on their screen, even in low light, and even if you use light colors like grey. This is especially important for text: The smaller the text, the higher its contrast to the background needs to be for it to be readable. The contrast ratio between background and foreground should be at least 2.5 for big text and at least 4 for small text. In addition to having a high contrast ratio, avoid complementary hues (e.g. red and green, orange, and blue) and bright colors for backgrounds. Use  this tool  to test your color contrast, the brightness difference, and if colors are “compliant”. Consider where your colors appear in relation to each other.  The smaller the areas on your chart and the bigger the distance between them, the harder it is to compare them. Consider giving small points or lines a high contrast in their hue or brightness, to make them easily distinguishable. However, big areas can handle toned-down colors with little contrast; especially if there is no other (background)color between these areas: Use intuitive colors.  When choosing a color palette, consider their meaning in the culture of your target audience. If possible, use colors that readers will associate with your data anyway, e.g. party colors: Republican = red, Democrats = blue; natural colors: forest = green, lake = blue; or learned colors: red = attention/stop/bad, green = good (to go). When it comes to color-encoding gender data, consider avoiding the stereotypical pink-blue combination. To not confuse your readers entirely, try a cold color for men (e.g. blue or purple) and a warmer color for women (e.g. yellow, orange or a warm green): Use light colors for low values and dark colors for high values.  When using color gradients, make sure that the bright colors represent low values, while the dark colors represent high values. This will be most intuitive for most readers: Don’t use a gradient color palette for categories and the other way round.  It might be tempting to use shades of one hue (e.g. blue) even for categories, to make your chart look less colorful. However, since many readers will associate dark colors with “more/high” and bright colors with “less/low”, such a color palette will imply a ranking of your categories. Use different hues (green, yellow, pink, etc.) for your categories to avoid that, and to be able to talk about these colors. Readers might be quicker at finding specific categories if you make their colors stand out with a different lightness or saturation, but note that your chart should explain why these colors stand out. If you find your chart too colorful, consider another chart type for your data. Use lightness to build gradients, not just hue.  When designing color gradients, lots of consideration is needed. If you’re unsure, use the defaults of our data visualization tool  Datawrapper , the  ColorBrewer  palettes or these  Carto gradients . If you do want to try your hand at it: Don’t place more than two hues with the same lightness in your gradient, but design it from a bright color (e.g. white) to a dark color (e.g. dark blue) in a consistent way. Your gradient should work in black and white, too. Gradients with much variation in lightness (like rainbow scales) can confuse readers: Consider using two hues for a gradient, not just one.  This is the next step to make your map or chart even more decipherable. Readers will be able to distinguish the colors on the gradient better if they are encoded through lightness  and  (two or three carefully selected) hue: Consider using diverging color gradients.  If you want to emphasize how a variable diverts from a baseline (say the national average), you may want to consider using a diverging palette. It’s important to use clearly distinguishable hues for both sides of the gradient. The center color should ideally be a light grey, not white: Consider color-blind people.  Using different lightnesses in your gradients and color palettes has the big advantage that readers with a color vision deficiency will still be able to distinguish your colors. There are  many  different types of color blindness: Use an  online tool  or  Datawrapper’s automatic colorblind-check  to make sure that color-blind users can distinguish the colors on your chart. To learn more, visit our three-part series on visualizing data for colorblind readers: part 1 , part 2 , part 3 . Want to know more? Rules for color usage in data visualization that Elijah learned while he and Susie Lu created the tool  Viz Palette , especially in the second part of the article. results.pageDescription: News, Analysen und Hintergründe – visuell und datenbasiert aufbereitet. Modernstes digitales Storytelling von NZZ Visuals.
results.evidenceText: Visuals – datengetriebene, visuelle Geschichten | NZZ Interaktiv : Drei tödliche Minuten in Krakau Der Anschlag in der zweitgrössten Stadt Polens war einer der schwersten der vergangenen Jahre in Mitteleuropa. Eine Rekonstruktion zeigt, wie schnell die Polizei den Täter stoppen konnte. Jan Ludwig, Samuel Meier, Franco Gervasi, Jasmine Jacot-Descombes 3 min Pro Artikel Im Westen Äthiopiens sammeln sich Truppen. Bringen sie eine Wende im Sudan-Krieg? Satellitenbilder und Videos deuten darauf hin, dass die Rapid Support Forces über eine äthiopische Armeebasis Nachschub erhalten. Doch ihre Offensive im sudanesischen Bürgerkrieg birgt Risiken. Samuel Meier, Ida Götz, Seda Motie 5 min Neandertaler hätten ihre Toten auf Blumen gebettet, hiess es. Das stimmt wohl nicht – stattdessen finden sich an den Knochen Spuren tödlicher Gewalt Im heutigen Kurdistan liegt eine der wichtigsten archäologischen Fundstellen für Frühmenschen: die Shanidar-Höhle. Immer wieder erbringt sie neue Erkenntnisse. Jetzt: ein durchlöchertes Schulterblatt und einen gespaltenen Zahn. Esther Widmann, Anja Lemcke (Infografik) 5 min Datenanalyse : Praktisch in den ganzen USA hat ein Sinneswandel stattgefunden – die Datenanalyse zum Wahlverhalten Die Demokraten können bei den Zwischenwahlen einen spektakulären Sieg einfahren. Unsere Datenanalyse zeigt, in welchen Countys der Meinungsumschwung besonders stark war, wer zu Hause blieb und welche Wählergruppen zu den Demokraten zurückkehrten. Nikolai Thelitz, Joana Kelén 3 min Interaktiv : Alle Angriffe und Rückeroberungen der letzten vier Kriegsjahre – klicken Sie sich durch unsere Karte Seit vier Jahren kartografiert die NZZ täglich den Krieg in der Ukraine. Klicken Sie sich durch alle wichtigen Ereignisse im russischen Angriffskrieg. NZZ Visuals 5 min Empfehlungen Angriff auf Iran: Die wichtigsten Karten und Grafiken zur aktuellen Lage Die USA haben im Nahen Osten eine massive Streitmacht zusammengezogen und rüsten für einen längeren Krieg. Doch Iran schlägt heftig zurück. Eine Übersicht. Julia Monn 5 min Visual Teams, Methoden und Styleguide Vom Tod Khameneis bis zu Raketen auf Dubai: was über die Folgen der Operation «Epic Fury» bekannt ist – und wie Iran sich rächt In mehreren Wellen greifen Amerika und Israel Ziele in Iran an. Teheran schlägt heftig zurück. Eine Übersicht über den ersten Kriegstag in Karten und Bildern. Eike Hoppmann, Julia Monn, Seda Motie, Roland Shaw 6 min Interaktiv : Wo würden Sie sparen, wenn Sie SRG-Generaldirektorin Susanne Wille wären? Probieren Sie es aus Am 8. März stimmt die Schweiz über die SRG-Initiative ab, die die Gebühren massiv senken will. Die SRG müsste ungefähr 750 Millionen Franken sparen. Entscheiden Sie selbst, wo Sie ansetzen würden. Andrea Brühlmann, Olivia Fischer, Samuel Tanner 2 min Alle Resultate zu den Abstimmungen in der Schweiz vom 27. September 2026 Die Schweizerinnen und Schweizer haben heute über die Neutralitätsinitiative und die Ernährungsinitiative abgestimmt. Auch in Zürich standen mehrere Volksentscheide an. Alle Resultate im Überblick. Nikolai Thelitz, Leila Epprecht 2 min Interaktiv : Linker Einheitsbrei im Zürcher Stadtparlament? Eine Analyse der Kandidierenden zeigt: Die SVP ist diverser als die SP Über tausend Personen kämpfen um einen Platz im Zürcher Stadtparlament. Diese 3-D-Visualisierung zeigt die Bewerber – und wie sie sich unterscheiden. Simon Huwiler, Cian Jochem 2 min «Le Constellation»: Schmale Fluchtwege und die Suche nach dem zweiten Ausgang Dieses 3-D-Modell zeigt, wo sich der zweite Ausgang befinden könnte. Und es liefert Hinweise darauf, wie es zur Tragödie im Wallis kommen konnte. Samuel Meier, Jonas Oesch, Simon Huwiler 5 min «Ich = smarte Assistentin» – wie eine Bankmitarbeiterin aus Zürich Jeffrey Epstein junge Frauen vermittelte Eine Russin führte über Jahre hinweg eine enge Verbindung mit Jeffrey Epstein. Sie stellte ihm junge Frauen vor – und erhielt Geld für ihre Ausbildung und einflussreiche Kontakte. Der Fall zeigt, wie Schuld und Abhängigkeit in Epsteins Umfeld verschwimmen. Florian Schoop, Eike Hoppmann, Forrest Rogers, Jasmine Rueegg (Illustration) 11 min Pro Artikel Eskalation in Reichweite: Wie sich die amerikanischen Streitkräfte um Iran formieren Die USA bündeln Kriegsschiffe, Kampfflugzeuge und Helikopter im Nahen Osten und im Indischen Ozean. Diese visuelle Analyse zeigt den Stand des Aufmarsches – und diskutiert die militärischen Optionen der Amerikaner gegen das Regime in Teheran. Samuel Meier, Jasmine Jacot-Descombes, Georg Häsler, Franco Gervasi 4 min Die Schweiz und die EU finanzieren in Griechenland gefängnisartige Asylzentren. Was passiert im Innern? Samos schockierte einst mit überfüllten, elenden Flüchtlingslagern. Heute steht auf der Insel eine stark gesicherte Anlage für Migranten. Die NZZ blickt hinter den Stacheldrahtzaun. NZZ-Redaktion 17 min Pro Artikel Wie ICE Tausende Menschen durch sein Haftsystem schleust Wer von der Einwanderungsbehörde festgenommen wird, landet in einem Netzwerk aus Zellen, Transportflugzeugen und Abschiebehallen. Unter Präsident Trump wird es massiv ausgebaut. Julia Monn, Cian Jochem, Jasmin Hegetschweiler, Andrea Brühlmann 5 min Neu im Ressort Pro Artikel Zürcher Startup baut KI-Mitarbeiter: «Die haben keine Launen und machen, was man ihnen sagt» Jetzt gibt es KI-Mitarbeiter mit Gesicht, E-Mail-Adresse und Monatslohn. Der Uhrenhersteller Breitling hat bereits einen künstlichen Controller im Einsatz. Die Gründer von Square8 sagen: «Irgendwann machen ‹AI Worker› jeden Job besser als Menschen.» Christin Severin, Jasmin Hegetschweiler 5 min Pro Artikel Im Sudan geraten Märkte zunehmend ins Visier von Drohnen Im Sudan kann schon der Gang zum Einkauf tödlich enden. Innerhalb einer Woche wurden zwei Märkte von Drohnen getroffen, mehr als 250 Menschen starben. Die Attacken sind Teil einer zunehmenden Welle tödlicher Drohnenangriffe. Seda Motie 3 min Die Saga vom Reiter, der Kopf und König verlor – und nun als Rächer aus der Schweiz nach Nigeria zurückkehrt Eine Geschichte über koloniales Raubgut und die Frage: Was bringt Sühne, wenn ein Verbrechen 130 Jahre zurückliegt? Giorgio Scherrer (Text), Jasmine Rueegg (Illustrationen) 12 min Wie konnte es erneut zu einem tödlichen Zugunglück in Spanien kommen? Eine visuelle Rekonstruktion Innert 17 Minuten passierten die Fehler, die zum verheerenden Aufprall von zwei Schnellzügen führten. Aufgezeichnete Funkgespräche deuten auf technisches und menschliches Versagen hin. Julia Monn, Cian Jochem, Jessica Eberhart 5 min Hat dieses Video die Massen in Frankreich für den 17. Oktober mobilisiert? Über eine halbe Million Menschen zog es an diesem Tag landesweit auf die Strassen. Wer nach dem Ursprung des Datums sucht, landet bei Tiktok – und stösst auf einige Merkwürdigkeiten. Eike Hoppmann, Seda Motie 6 min Von Trump bis Milei: Auf diese Freunde können sich die Bolsonaros stützen Flávio Bolsonaro hat Brasilien nach der Wahlniederlage gegen Lula verlassen. Nun setzt der Clan auf ein Netzwerk, das er über Jahre im Ausland aufgebaut hat. Alexander Busch, Cian Jochem 1 min IBAN-Nummern, Kinderfotos und private Adressen: Hacker bieten Hockey-Daten für 250 Franken an Hacker haben hochsensible Daten des Schweizer Eishockeyverbands erbeutet. Die NZZ hat einen Teil davon überprüft und brisante Informationen gefunden. Simon Huwiler 3 min Pro Artikel Verfolgungsjagd im All: Russischer Militärsatellit riskiert eine Kollision mit einem US-Satelliten Wochenlang verändert ein russischer Militärsatellit seinen Kurs, bis er einem amerikanischen Radarsatelliten gefährlich nahe kommt. War die Annäherung gezielt? Die NZZ hat das Manöver anhand der Flugbahnen rekonstruiert. Jessica Eberhart, Jasmine Rueegg, Leila Epprecht 3 min Es begann auf dem Meeresgrund. Die bisher unbekannte Geschichte des Lebens Bis heute hält sich die Vorstellung, das Leben auf der Erde sei in einer Ursuppe entstanden. Doch immer mehr Hinweise sprechen dafür, dass es in winzigen Gesteinsporen am Meeresgrund begonnen hat. Dort hat sich vor 4 Milliarden Jahren die Lebensflamme entzündet, und sie hat unseren Planeten seither grundlegend verändert. NZZ-Redaktion 22 min Der Abstieg des Goldhasen Schokolade von Lindt & Sprüngli war das Premiumprodukt für die Massen schlechthin. Doch die Verkaufszahlen sinken. Für die Konsumenten ist die Marke gerade vor allem eines: zu teuer. Valentina Rötheli, Elena Oberholzer (Text), Florian Seliger (Grafiken) 6 min Datenanalyse : Pro Artikel Begonnen hat alles mit Schülerprotesten. Doch sind französische Schulen wirklich so schlecht? Im internationalen Vergleich fallen besonders die grossen Klassen und unzufriedene Lehrpersonen auf. OECD-Daten zeigen aber, dass Frankreich bei vielen Bildungsindikatoren nicht schlechter abschneidet als andere grosse europäische Länder. Roland Shaw, Florian Seliger 6 min Pro Artikel Russland nimmt Kiews Brücken ins Visier. Eine Analyse der Angriffe in Videos und Karten Seit einigen Wochen greift Russland gezielt die Dnipro-Übergänge in Kiew an. Bis jetzt halten die Brücken stand, doch die Gefahr ist eine andere. Eike Hoppmann, Jonas Oesch 2 min Pilze: Das geheime Untergrundnetzwerk des Waldes Endlich ist wieder Pilzsaison. Was da im Körbchen von Sammlern landet, sind nur die sichtbaren Fruchtkörper einer unterirdischen Lebensgemeinschaft von Pilz und Baum. Dahinter verbirgt sich das sogenannte «Wood Wide Web», ein Netzwerk, ohne das unser Planet kaum bewohnbar wäre. Ein virtueller Waldspaziergang. Georg Rüschemeyer, Ida Götz 2 min Viel Geld für Waffen und doch verwundbar: weshalb die Huthi-Raketen Saudiarabien empfindlich treffen können Das Königreich gibt jährlich etwa 80 Milliarden Dollar für das Militär aus. Doch auch modernste Waffensysteme brauchen Nachschub – und Fachleute, die sie bedienen. Julia Monn, Joana Kelén, Leila Epprecht 3 min Pro Artikel Die Stadt Rafah gibt es nicht mehr Schulen und Tankstellen, Moscheen und Wohnhäuser: Mehr als zwei Jahre nach der israelischen Offensive in der Grossstadt im Gazastreifen sind fast alle Gebäude zerstört. Aktuelle Satellitenbilder zeigen eine Wüste aus Trümmern. Jasmine Jacot-Descombes, Samuel Meier, Nicolas Staub, Anja Lemcke 2 min Die Schweiz-Verbindungen des Ex-BND-Chefs August Hanning Nach seiner Pensionierung war Hanning für drei Schweizer Firmen tätig. Hinweise auf einen Zusammenhang mit den Spionagevorwürfen gibt es gegenwärtig nicht – wohl aber auf seine Verwicklung in einen anderen Fall. Eike Hoppmann 5 min Auch Moleküle können links oder rechts sein, mit teilweise gefährlichen Konsequenzen: Der Chemienobelpreis geht an zwei Forscher aus Frankreich und Japan Henri Kagan und Kenso Soai haben Reaktionen entdeckt, mit denen man selektiv nur eine dieser spiegelbildlichen Varianten herstellen kann. Das ist wichtig für die Entwicklung von Medikamenten. Stephanie Lahrtz, Georg Rüschemeyer, Jasmine Rueegg (Infografik) 4 min Ernie und Bert sei Dank: Der Neutrino-Forscher Francis Halzen erhält den Physiknobelpreis Halzen erhält den Preis für seine entscheidenden Beiträge zum Neutrino-Observatorium Ice Cube, mit dem sich schnelle Geisterteilchen aus den Tiefen des Alls nachweisen lassen. Christian Speicher 4 min Pro Artikel In Ceuta schlafen noch immer Tausende Migranten auf der Strasse Improvisierte Zeltlager, Obdachlose und Müll prägen das Stadtbild weiterhin, die Unterkünfte reichen nicht aus. Introduction to Data Visualization Planning a Data Visualization Designing Effective Data Visualizations Choosing an Appropriate Visual Encoding Color in Data Visualizations Data Visualization Design Resources Network Visualization Scientific Visualization Workshops, Tutorials, and Resources Data Visualization Best Practices 1. Know your audience. 2. Know you message. 3. Adapt your visualization scale to the presentation medium. 4. Avoid chartjunk (Keep it simple). 5. Use color effectively. 6. Avoid the default settings. Ask Me Peter Lawson Data and Visualization Librarian Email Me   Contact: Data Services dataservices@jhu.edu Choosing an Appropriate Visual Encoding Data visualization relies on communication through perception . A good data visualization can exploit the natural tendency of the human visual system to recognize structure and patterns. The brain can process information faster and more efficiently when it is in a visual format . Key to achieving this is the choice of visual encodings for your data that correspond to preattentive attributes . Preattentive attributes are visual attributes, including size, color, shape, and position that are processed at a high speed by the visual system. Consider the images below, what stands out to you in each image? Was the red dot in the color hue figure immediately apparent? That is preattentive processing at work. Image Source: https://help.tableau.com/current/blueprint/en-us/bp_why_visual_analytics.htm Precision of Quantitative Information Attribute Example Natural Interpretation Highly Precise                           Length                                        Longer = Greater Position Higher = Greater Imprecise Width Wider = Greater Size Larger = Greater Intensity Darker = Greater     Images adapted from: https://help.tableau.com/current/blueprint/en-us/bp_why_visual_analytics.htm Table adapted from: Few, S. (2009). Now you see it: Simple visualization techniques for quantitative analysis (p. 41). Oakland, CA: Analytics Press. Color in Data Visualizations Choosing a Color Palette Your selection of a color palette in your data visualization will depend on properties of your data. The three primary types of color palettes include: Type of Color Palette Description of Use Example Qualitative Palette C ategorical data that does not have an inherent ordering. Sequential Palette Data that is numeric, or has a natural ordering. Diverging Palette Numeric data that diverges from a center value. Image Source: https://medium.com/nightingale/how-to-choose-the-colors-for-your-data-visualizations-50b2557fa335 Color in Data Visualization Resources ColorBrewer2 A tool for generating sequential, diverging, and qualitative color palettes. Originally intended for cartography, this tool can be used for generating color palettes for a range of data visualizations. Data Visualization Design Resources Data Viz Catalogue The Data Visualization Catalogue provides a useful taxonomy of visualizations, organized by functions such as comparisons, proportions, and distributions. It is a good place to start if you are not certain what data visualization is right for you. Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures A useful article published in PLOS Computational Biology which compresses data visualization best practices into ten simple rules.
